items.title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
items.content: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as: [...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others: Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75 Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50 >200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50 Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50 But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models: The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement: It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. (That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!) Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles . The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response. Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too: The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder , which is 40x the price of Muse Ember. items.title: [AINews] Fable 5.2 retakes World #1 LLM spot as $ANT IPO roadshow begins
items.content: On Friday, we asked Jamin Ball what comes next for Anthropic’s IPO . On Monday the roadshow started and Anthropic shipped the long-anticipated next-version of Claude Fable and Mythos . Of course, it is the new top model in the world, taking back Opus 5.5’s #1 spot from Gemini 4 Carbon which had its brief moment in the sun (10 days). View post on X ↗ Fable comes with a 20% per token price cut… but is more token hungry, as both SemiAnalysis GDPx and Artificial Analysis agree: Fable 5.1 cost $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 costs $8 and $40 . Yet on GDPx, a benchmark of professional tasks, SemiAnalysis paid $88.15 per task, up from $67.16 . The run logs give a clue. Where Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 would try about 20 test cases, 5.2 sometimes wrote hundreds or thousands and spun up subagents to check its work independently. All that checking helped Fable take first place at 16.4% . You pay for the checks either way. Which effort setting should you put in production? On FrontierCode 2.0, Anthropic reports that Fable at High matched Opus 5.5 at Max for about half the cost per task… but don’t talk about Fable at Max. AI News for 11/07/2026-11/09/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Top Story: Claude Fable 5.2 / Mythos 5.2 Benchmarks, Economics, Restrictions, and First Impressions What happened Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, claiming both are "a step above Opus 5.5 in almost all the capabilities we evaluated." It tops most independent leaderboards. It also arrives with deliberate RSI nerfs, heavier per-task costs and restricted subscription access. Launch claims. @claudeai announced the pair as built for "the most daunting technical challenges," with gains in coding, reasoning and vision. @marktenenholtz flagged unusual system-card phrasing: "The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2." That implies a single shared base model. Vendor-reported headline numbers , per @kimmonismus : Up to 30% faster output than the 5.1 models. On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 at High matched Opus 5.5 at Max for about half the cost per task, and at Xhigh it was the top released model. 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents formalized the existing proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours. Opus 5.5 completed 26% in 18 hours on the same setup. Mythos 5.2 accurately modeled 28 of 34 gene-therapy capsids. Alignment was at or above recent Claude models, with external pre-release testing. Default effort. Medium is the default effort in the Claude apps and Claude Code. Pricing. $8/$40 per 1M input/output tokens, 20% below Fable 5.1's $10/$50 ( @jaminball , @arena ). The rest of the spec, per Artificial Analysis : Cache writes cost $10 (5-minute TTL) or $16 (1-hour TTL); cache reads cost $0.20. 1M-token context with text and image input. Five effort levels: low, medium, high, xhigh, max. Long-horizon demos from Anthropic. An OS was built from an empty folder by 1,000+ subagents over 8 days. It boots on a laptop and has its own kernel, disk/keyboard/network drivers, persistent storage, windowing, login, an installer and built-in Claude ( @kimmonismus ). Fable designed three working electronic devices from a short prompt ( @kimmonismus ). It proposed untested chemical synthesis routes. It improved on listed solutions to 72 open optimization problems. @RLanceMartin published the safety-bounded scaling write-up for the 1,000-agent FLT run. Subscription access. Ultra and Team Premium users get Fable "resets" scaled by tenure: 1 reset under 6 months, 2 for 6–12 months, 3 above 12 months, usable until March 8 ( @ClaudeDevs ; echoed by @bcherny and @edwinarbus ). Pro and Team Standard get a one-week trial capped at half the weekly limit, plus one reset. Fable can only consume 50% of a weekly limit. Data retention. Fable 5.2 requires data retention by default so Anthropic's safety classifiers can run. Zero data retention is available only to eligible enterprise customers ( @code ). Rollout, day one: Cursor ( @cursor_ai ). GitHub Copilot / VS Code, where it "solved more tasks than Fable 5.1 while using fewer steps and tool calls" ( @code ). Perplexity Computer (Pro/Max) and Search (Max) ( @perplexity_ai ). @AravSrinivas made it his "new default." Factory ( @factory ). Hermes Agent via Nous Portal and OpenRouter ( @Teknium ). Arena ( @arena ) and DesignArena ( @grx_xce ). Official model-selection guide. @ClaudeDevs published guidance on Fable vs Opus vs Sonnet vs Haiku. It covers when to raise effort instead of switching models, and when to push subagents to smaller models. Independent evals (facts) Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 ( @ArtificialAnlys , breakdown ): Fable 5.2 is #1 at 65 (max) . Fable 5.2 (max) — Index score 65 Gemini 4 Carbon (high) — Index score 60 Opus 5.5 (max) — Index score 59 GPT-6 Astra (max) — Index score 57 Fable 5.1 (max) — Index score 49 New records: HLE-Diamond — Fable 5.2 80% · Previous best 69% AA-Omniscience v1.1 — Fable 5.2 67 · Previous best 54 Terminal-Bench-Science — Fable 5.2 73% · Previous best 65% CritPt v2 hard — Fable 5.2 77% · Previous best 72% FrontierCode 2.0 — Fable 5.2 49% · Previous best 46% (Opus 5.5) Weaker spots: AA-Briefcase: 1785 Elo, within the confidence interval of Opus 5.5 (1800) and behind Sonnet 5.5 (1813). GDP.pdf: 24% all-pass vs 26% for Opus 5.5. Terminal-Bench 4.0: 60%, level with Opus 5.5 and behind Kimi K3.1 Pro (67%), Gemini 4 Carbon (65%) and Sonnet 5.5 (64%). AutomationBench-AA: 76%, ahead of Opus 5.5 (70%) but behind Gemini 4 Carbon (78%). Efficiency: At high and xhigh it scores 62 using about 98k output tokens per task, vs 173k for Opus 5.5 max. At max, cost per task is about $26.5, roughly 2.6× Opus 5.5 ($10.0) and 2× Fable 5.1 ($12.99). Epoch Capabilities Index ( @EpochAIResearch ): a record 174

items.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
items.content: Claude Fable 5.2 responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, when a prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, the model tended to add to the existing structure, even when that repeated existing code. [...] If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model merged repeated code in about half of the tries with this sentence, and in under a tenth of the tries without it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: prompt-engineering , anthropic , generative-ai , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

items.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
items.content: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such. Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced. How it works When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract: We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting. That sounded exactly like what we needed to build! Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js ), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server. When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep. How I built it I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session , which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository: Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though? That got me this problem.md file . As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file. The research looked good, so I told it: Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet. I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released , and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces. I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran. This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients. items.title: What Frontier Labs Buy: A Data Deep Dive with Handshake AI — Garrett Lord & Team
items.content: This is our first Latent Space deep dive with an AI data company . In roughly a year, Handshake’s AI training business went from launch to $1 billion in gross annualized revenue . What are frontier labs buying at that scale? What evals are models still nowhere close to human level on? Garrett Lord brought the people who build these reinforcement learning environments to show us. For the first time, we are walking through them live! To cover the scope of Handshake, we had to produce a very special joint podcast across our Science/Engineering/Research/Finance podcast hosts, because Handshake’s business runs across all these and more. Watch for three segments after the general intro: Finance. In the finance demo, the agent has to find its assignment in a bank’s email, work out which files govern the deal, and deliver a workbook. Watch what happens to one line in the client’s email about existing goodwill. The agent carries the number into Python and subtracts it. Collin points out that the model can explain the tax treatment when you ask it directly. The mistake comes when it has to recognize that this particular line of code is where the rule applies. Bio. Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller show us VIALS, Handshake’s benchmark for interpreting the images scientists use at work. Nick puts nine slides of brain-tumor tissue on screen and asks which two show the most advanced vessel necrosis. Give yourself a moment before his answer. Nick picks H and I. The model picks those two and adds G. Watching Nick point to what’s missing from the tissue is more instructive than seeing the score. Coding. In a simulated file-access task, the team can inspect which files an agent read, whether it checked the copies, and what it did to the shell history afterward. A transcript of the agent’s final reply would miss most of what Steve Kelling and Nishant Ranka are evaluating. Who’s in the room 🟣 AI data business — Garrett Lord, Sahil Bhaiwala and Nishant Ranka open and close the episode on the market for expert data. 🌸 Life sciences — Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller put the gel and brain-tissue tasks on screen. 🟢 Finance — Collin Schweiker and Sahil Bhaiwala take us through Project Falcon and its Excel grader. 🟠 Alignment — Steve Kelling and Nishant Ranka follow the agent’s tool calls through the safety simulations. Show notes ATLAS-Finance — Explore the benchmark for agents working across a simulated bank’s inboxes, documents, and financial models. Inside a bank — Handshake traces a separate published deal, Project Osprey, from the client’s email to a grading decision. The deal on screen in our interview is Project Falcon. VIALS sample tasks — Try the scientific image questions, including the gel and brain-tissue tasks from the episode. How Handshake trained a model to read scientific figures — The team describes using intermediate image descriptions to train and evaluate a vision-language model. items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
items.content: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: < details > < summary > Claude Opus 5.5 </ summary > < h2 > The hook </ h2 > Plugins implement < code > register_agent_reference_types(datasette) </ code > ... </ details > When rendered, it looks like this : Crucially, <details><summary> is supported in GitHub Markdown . You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow. I've started using this for my AI-generated pull requests. The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what's going on - the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed. I'll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature. The full agent-written essay then follows in a <details><summary> . I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on - "Claude Opus 5.5 Medium" for example. My PRs don't feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details. I don't always write the introduction myself - sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time. Here are some recent examples where I've used this pattern, including the opener I used: datasette PR #3052: Redesign row page as a vertical list of fields - "The row page showed its single row as a one-row table. For wide tables, like a 46-column GitHub repos table, that scrolled far off to the right and left most of the page blank." (then a screenshot) datasette PR #3043: Pagination bar showing which rows are on the current page - "Table pages that span more than one page now make it obvious where you are, and offer navigation at the top of the page as well as the bottom." (plus screenshot) datasette PR #3042: Load edit-tools.js on demand via a small loader - " edit-tools.js (~220KB) was loaded on every table, row and database page, even for users who couldn't edit anything. Now only load it for users who can edit when they first interact with an edit feature (including mouse over an edit link)." datasette-agent PR #51: register_agent_reference_types plugin hook - "Lets plugins add their own kinds of item to the # tagging in the chat composer using a new register_agent_reference_types(datasette) plugin hook." - pictured above. llm PR #1838: Add llm openai endpoint add/list/remove/path commands - "Adds commands for managing the records in extra-openai-models.yaml , so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can be saved from the command line instead of by hand-editing YAML." - then copied --help output. The mnemonic I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags - is it <details><summary> or <summary><details> ? Here are two tricks that helped me. First, and most obviously, the <summary> is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That's the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand - the <details> element must then wrap everything else. An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as "details-summary". "details-summary" is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of "summary-details". Say "details-summary" out loud just a few times and you'll never forget the order of the tags again. (I still wish GitHub would add a button to their Markdown editor for this - partly to save me painstakingly typing it on my mobile keyboard, and partly to help spread the word to more GitHub users that this feature exists.) items.title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
items.content: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted : I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted: Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation And it did, using "Clinger's fast path": Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better: first C new C rusqlite sqlite-loadable Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in simonw/research by prompting this: Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder Here's the resulting report . items.title: How Stanford Teaches AI-Native Engineering — Mihail Eric, Monaco
items.content: The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers . Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us are asking at work: what should a software engineer actually learn now? Mihail Eric has two places to test his answer. He teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, where his colleagues use coding agents to ship software and investigate outages. I asked him to take us through the syllabus, then tell us which parts survived contact with his own engineering team. This is also meant as a preview for all of you joining us in San Francisco for AIE Code next week, as required knowledge for all the conversations with the speakers, sponsors and attendees you’re about to have. datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
items.content: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means for everyone else their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! items.content: My comment on Terry Pratchett's Study — Hacker News. Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich: https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin... But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it. items.content: Fabian Theis has been one of the key players in the various iterations of the Virtual Cell concept and initiatives. It is not hyperbole at all to say that his lab has been pushing the frontier of algorithms to understand multi-scale, multi-modal (”multiomics”), time-varying biological data. Indeed, he has shaped the large scale vision and data collection through his leadership at Helmholtz, various startups and probably at Biohub itself. Watch the full episode on YouTube… Much of the recent attention in AI x Bio has been on protein and molecular design. AlphaFold, ESM and BioHub , Chai , Leash , Isomporphic, Boltz , Genesis , Octant, Baker Lab, and many many more. After a lot of initial excitement, Virtual Cell projects have received less attention, due in no small part to questions about the effectiveness of large-scale models in solving even basic Virtual Cell problems. A $1.8B bet The Biohub announcement a few weeks ago got a lot of press for the (really) big numbers: $1.8B of commitments [1] from Biohub, NIH, DOE, Google and Meta. The discussion cites new imaging and measurement capabilities, generating large data sets and making the data available for training AI. View post on X ↗ But why are these organizations doubling down on these big bets now? They have been in the works for years now, what is going on that makes now the moment to push? New measurement capabilities and scale infrastructure, are now coming online that make Biohub’s push likely lead to big impact on science. DOE and NIH are developing lab-in-the-loop automation capabilities at scale. Google is scaling and broadening its connectomics capabilities ( episode coming soon!). Biohub itself has worked with various labs to develop and improve imaging platforms like laser phase plate microscopy, light sheet microscopy and advanced post-processing for regular microscopes that reveal deep phenotypic data. These technologies are quickly maturing, and will likely play a big part in the Biohub initiative. Virtual cells struggle This kind of multi-scale, multi-modal data looks a lot like the data Fabian has made a career out modeling. On the other hand Virtual Cell modeling has run into problems that have dampened excitement about systems biology. The 2025 Arc Virtual Cell Challenge shined a light on the problem: a slew of papers pointed out that constant baselines (not even linear!) often beat sophisticated models for “Perturbation Prediction”. If you change the inputs or programming of a cell (via gene editing, drugs or other environmental factors), how will the cell change it’s “state”. The disappointing finding is that many models fail to beat even the most basic basic baselines 🤦‍♂️. The situation is not actually so bad: This excellent paper show that many existing evaluation metrics are poorly calibrated: they can reward an uninformative mean prediction because most genes barely change. With better-calibrated metrics, deep learning models can outperform the mean baseline. The problem is the problem Nonetheless, Fabian Theis believes that perturbation prediction under the existing data sets just isn’t a hard enough problem to warrant complex algorithms. Instead we should be focused on exactly the problems that Biohub just announce an $1.8B data collection effort around: using large, high precision, multi-scale, co-registered biological data to predict the evolution of molecules → cells → niches → tissues → organs → organisms, and how all these scales effect one another. This is a happy situation: at this very moment, AI is enabling us to tackle dramatically larger problems, and this problem is very, very big. We lack understanding of the “scale interfaces” between these different different “domains of applicability,” and we lack the data. The Biohub initiative aims to solve the data problem. Fabian Theis has been working on the algorithms to model these larger problems for years. How do the other cells near me change my state? What happens to a distribution of cells from a perturbation? How do I perturb a cell to get it into the state I want? These are increasingly complex questions that are building towards a lab-in-the-loop and large scale experimentation, and (actually) require increasingly complex models. Models drive precision medicine Fabian’s labs and initiatives have been also investing heavily: the Computational Health Center at Helmholtz combines AI, molecular data, medical imaging, genomics, and clinical data to develop predictive and mechanistic models for precision medicine. The Institute of Computational Biology develops statistical and dynamical models integrating biological information from single-cell time series through population-scale omics data. Given his drivers seat at the frontier, we were so excited for the opportunity to get an hour of his time to understand how Fabian Theis is thinking about Virtual Cells when the concept of what is difficult is changing so quickly. Greg Brockman cites about $1,000 per vulnerability ( post ). Cost trajectory : One comparison puts GPT‑5.6 Sol at 166 vulnerabilities for about $500k in July 2026, against 948 for about $1.2M with the new model ( comparison ). One commenter estimates the real internal cost is far below the API list price; this is an unverified estimate ( estimate ). Modal describes it as a post-training update to K3, with expanded RL for coding, financial research and long-horizon agentic work. It accepts text and images and has 1M context ( Modal ). Specs : The model has 2.8T total parameters with 104B active ( Ollama ). One commenter credits gated sparse attention for gains in intelligence and efficiency over K3 ( comment ). Independent signal : On Agent Arena it ranks #1 among open models and #13 overall, with +5.1% net improvement across more than 17.5K agentic sessions. One user reports that on an internal SRE-agent eval it uses more tokens but delivers "shockingly good" quality ( report ). Prime Intellect ran the pretraining clusters and cites 16x pretraining compute efficiency ( Prime Intellect ). On the scaling ladder, a new architecture on the same data as Olmo3 gave about a 3x gain, and a new dataset on the same architecture gave about 4x ( analysis ). It is Cognition's first model with a mid-training stage and was built in 6 weeks ( Silas Alberti ). Weights policy : Weights are not public. Cognition plans a secure weight-sharing program for partners and researchers and cites cyber-misuse risk ( details ). Availability : It is free through November for Devin Pro, Max and Teams users ( pricing ). Tencent Hy4 : Tencent reports 75.2 on APEX-Agents against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash's 72.1/72.9. However it is still a big wakeup moment and has had multiple independent replications by now that it is not worth either doing some kind of retraction or a followup title story saying it was bogus. Instead today we’re featuring AI Engineer Shanghai and also sharing an exclusive interview on the history of Latent Space ! AI News for 11/02/2026-11/03/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Weight-Space Programming: Frontier Models Reading and Writing Neural Network Weights Core claim and replications : Several groups report that frontier LLMs can generate or edit small networks' weights directly, without gradient training or tools. Cross-generation replication : Alex Krentsel's replication of MIT's experiment found a sharp capability jump across model generations; the latest models generated Breakout networks scoring up to 22× an RL-trained baseline ( summary ). Hugging Face reproduction : Hugging Face reproduced the paper with ML Intern, its open-source AI-research harness, and released the model and a demo ( NielsRogge ). Hand-written classifier : A user had Fable hand-write a 100K-parameter network that classifies real versus fake legal citations, reportedly outperforming a trained version ( jacsebl ). Legora's CTO highlighted the result ( mstockton ). Astra's Qwen edit, reconstructed : GPT-6 Astra edited 131,072 weights in Qwen3.5-0.8B without backprop, raising MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1%. A Zhihu reconstruction from the logs shows the gain is narrower than the headline ( ZhihuFrontier ): Failure mode : 576 of 579 repaired answers had originally hit the 32K-token limit because of looping. Method : Astra derived a "repetition direction" from contrastive looping/productive contexts, located it mainly in the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted 6× the projection from the top 64 aligned neurons per layer. Held-out result : Accuracy rose from 10.6% to 60.4% on 1,152 held-out problems. Most of the gain is existing reasoning that can now finish. Laptop reproduction : Simon Willison reports that Qwen 3.8 27B achieved the same weight-interpretation feat on his laptop after 45+ minutes ( simonw ). Skeptical readings : Baselines : Critics say the big claims lack competent baselines, the Qwen result is bug-fixing rather than recursive self-improvement, and the thread overclaims ( paul_cal ). Benchmark overfitting : Fitting weights directly against a benchmark is "essentially meaningless," as the nesformer Mario example shows ( dbreunig ). Mechanism : One thread asks whether models mainly read the first and last layers, which map to known inputs and outputs ( ravfogel ). Interpretability takeaway : Another view is that the real lesson is how effectively coding agents use mechanistic-interpretability tools ( jbhuang0604 ). Optimistic framing : Supporters frame the work as meta-learning finally working and treat weight optimization as structured-text optimization. How big is the open model economy today?
items.content: My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption are incredibly imprecise. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access. The primary question I wanted to address today is: What is the market for open model inference? Is it growing? Is it a rounding error relative to OpenAI/Anthropic? Share I’ve been building the best measurements I can here, primarily using the open model inference startups Baseten, Fireworks, and Together AI as the bellwethers here (along with the open model share of OpenRouter’s token volume, which they thankfully report in their API). The hyperscalers also likely have a major footprint here, e.g. Amazon Bedrock and Azure’s model garden, but I haven’t seen them break down usage by model category. The startups’ fates are much more directly correlated with the success of open model inference as a category. For the latest data, we can start with a slide from my talk on the open model economy (recording here ). These are the public disclosures from the open model startups on their token volume, over time, log-scale. This shows near-exponential growth, before the uptick that would follow GLM 5.2’s step change in open agents . For example, Fireworks announced at their first company conference this week that they’re serving more than 40T tokens per day to customers’ customized models. This is just one slice of their inference, a vertical that they said grew over 2x from this summer, so I would expect their total number this fall to be well above 100T tokens when we get the next update. My first instinct with these numbers has been to ground them versus any closed model or hyperscale company we can, at least in terms of token volume. Thankfully, Google releases token volumes for the entire platform and API usage in their earnings reports. Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
items.content: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I'm going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it's an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: breakout/prompt.txt freeway/prompt.txt pacman/prompt.txt pong/prompt.txt I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \ -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here's what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That's still my favorite model to run on my own laptop - it's just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \ llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \ -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here's the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. Confidence: 72% This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong ( reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. Description: The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. Confidence: 75% And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game.
